name: Jade Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the free-range egg side at Ashby Farm, two sheds with thirty-two thousand hens, plus we grow some of our own wheat for the feed. I'm in at six, walk both sheds, check the water lines, the ventilation and the camera alerts on my phone. Then it's the packing room, the grader and whatever the supermarket wants that week. Bird flu season, which is basically all winter now, means boots, disinfectant and a lot of worrying.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly. The sheds have cameras that flag hens behaving oddly, and I use an AI assistant every day for feed costings, staff rotas and writing emails to the packer. I set most of it up myself, the owners just sign the cheques. My partner Sam works at the feed mill and jokes that I'd marry the grader if I could.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When the flock's healthy, laying well and the grader's humming, it's really satisfying. I like solving things. I hate bird flu and I hate the egg price being set by people who've never cleaned a shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Hmm. I'd be surprised, honestly, given what I already use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but not a revolution, which is fair. I'd tell other poultry people to use it for the boring stuff, costings, records, rotas. Online I'd probably post a few practical tips in the egg producers' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think it's still worth it for me, because I already save maybe five hours a week. But I'd be a bit sad, because I had plans that needed it to get better, like a robot that collects floor eggs. Those are the eggs that cost us the most time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what I've got and get better at it. I'd put some savings into a little egg vending hut at the farm gate, which works with or without fancy AI. And I'd keep pushing the owners to add a third shed while interest rates are reasonable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a good year with no surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the egg vending hut.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a shed with a fridge and a card reader, nothing clever. The farm on the main road into town does one and it takes about three hundred a week. I'd do mine with a bit of honey and our own flour too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the egg price is set by people who've never cleaned a shed. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket buyers, mostly, and the big packers. I don't hate them, it's a business. I just think if they spent a week in a shed in January, they'd pay a bit more.

S0.say: She'd say AI is useful but not a revolution and tell other poultry farmers to use it for costings, records and rotas, posting practical tips in the egg producers' group.
S0.think: She'd still find it worthwhile, saving about five hours a week, but would be disappointed that plans needing better robots, like collecting floor eggs, wouldn't happen.
S0.do: Keeps using and improving her current tools, puts savings into a farm-gate egg vending hut selling eggs, honey and flour, and pushes the owners to add a third shed while rates are reasonable.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a good year with no surprises.
S0.quote: I just think if they spent a week in a shed in January, they'd pay a bit more.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is a confident daily AI user who sees the plateau as a small letdown. Her side business is low-tech and grounded. Her view of buyers is critical but not angry, which fits her centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I'm basically already living in, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that adapt will be fine and farms that don't will struggle. I'd say it at the producers' meeting and I'd offer to show people what I've set up. I'd also say government should help with training costs, because not everyone can teach themselves like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd do well. I'm the one who knows the systems, and the owners know it. The two older lads in the packing room, Derek and Phil, would be the ones at risk, and I'd feel bad about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owners to fund a floor-egg robot and an automatic grader upgrade this year, with a business case I'd write myself. I'd negotiate a pay rise or a small share in the egg business, in writing. And I'd start charging other farms a day rate to set up their camera systems, as a side thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little uneasy about Derek and Phil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Derek and Phil, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Derek's sixty-two, so maybe he'd take early retirement and be glad of it. Phil's forty and he's got kids. I'd try to train him on the grader so he's the person who fixes it, not the person it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a share in the business. How would the owners take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd grumble, then probably agree, because they know I could walk to any of five other units within twenty miles. That's the nice thing about having savings and options. I don't have to be polite about it.

S1.say: She'd say farms that adapt will be fine and those that don't will struggle, offer to show other producers her setup, and support government help with training for those who can't teach themselves.
S1.think: She expects to do well as the person who knows the systems. She worries about the two older packing room workers, Derek and Phil.
S1.do: Writes a business case for a floor-egg robot and grader upgrade this year, negotiates a pay rise or small written share in the egg business, and starts charging other farms a day rate to set up camera systems.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, a little uneasy about her two colleagues.
S1.quote: That's the nice thing about having savings and options. I don't have to be polite about it.
S1.fieldNote: Jade is open about using her savings and local job options as bargaining power. She automates eagerly but tries to move Phil into a maintenance role rather than out the door. Her consultancy idea shows how fast she spots side income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? OK. That's the one where even I get nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stay calm and make sure food keeps being produced safely, with proper welfare rules for robot-run sheds. I'd also say the government will have to support people who lose jobs, at least for a while. I'd say it straight, no drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a robot that can do anything doesn't need a me to set it up. My whole edge is being early, and in two years everyone's early at once. I'd go from the clever one to the expensive one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd try to buy a proper share of Ashby's egg business, or my own small unit, so I own the sheds the robots work in. I'd use my savings and probably borrow. I'd keep the vending hut and use AI to run it with zero staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, I've got money and options, but my stomach would be in knots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes my plan from 'be the best worker' to 'be an owner, fast'. Two years is enough to buy something. It's not enough to train for something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't borrowing risky if nobody knows what happens to prices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, very. I'd lie awake about that. But if I don't own anything, I'm just a person in a world that doesn't need workers, and that sounds worse.

S2.say: She'd call for calm and for food to stay safe, with proper welfare rules for robot-run sheds, and say the government would have to support people who lose work for a while.
S2.think: She thinks a robot that can do anything doesn't need her to set it up; her edge is being early and in two years everyone is early. She'd go from the clever one to the expensive one.
S2.do: Moves at once to buy a real share of the egg business or her own small unit using savings and a loan, so she owns the sheds the robots work in, and runs her vending hut with AI and no staff.
S2.feel: Anxious with her stomach in knots, though not panicking because she has money and options.
S2.quote: My whole edge is being early, and in two years everyone's early at once. I'd go from the clever one to the expensive one.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture flips Jade's strategy from skill to ownership. She is clear-eyed that borrowing is risky but sees owning nothing as worse. Her cushion keeps her below alarm, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels like something I could actually ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and farms should plan now. I'd run a few evening sessions at the producers' group on what's coming and what's worth buying. I'd say the government should set clear rules early so people can make decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about perfect for me. I'd have time to be the person who installs and runs the robots for a few years, earn well and build up money. Then by 2031 I'd want to own the place, or part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd get the floor-egg robot in and write up results for other farms, and charge for consulting. Over years two and three I'd buy into Ashby's egg side or a small unit nearby. I'd keep the vending hut, and Sam and I would hold off on a bigger house until we know where it's heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but excited. Like the first day of a new flock coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on a bigger house. Is that a sacrifice for Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. He'd like a garden and a dog. But he also works at the feed mill, and if every farm automates, the mill changes too. We'd decide together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Derek and Phil in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Phil to learn the robots with me now, not in year four. And I'd tell Derek to enjoy his retirement, honestly. He's earned it.

S3.say: She'd say five years is short but workable, run evening sessions at the producers' group on what's worth buying, and ask the government to set clear rules early.
S3.think: She thinks five years is close to ideal for her: a few years installing and running robots and earning well, then owning all or part of a unit by 2031.
S3.do: Installs the floor-egg robot in year one and sells consulting to other farms, buys into the egg business or a nearby unit in years two and three, and delays a bigger house with her partner.
S3.feel: Anxious but excited, like a new flock arriving.
S3.quote: Five years is about perfect for me.
S3.fieldNote: Jade treats five years as a business plan: earn as an installer, then become an owner. Her partner's job at the feed mill adds a second household risk she hadn't mentioned before. She again tries to bring Phil along early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's loads. That's a whole business built and running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say with ten years, any farm that gets caught out has only itself to blame, and I'd mean it kindly. I'd keep running sessions for other producers. I'd want the government to make a clear plan for rural jobs, but I wouldn't expect miracles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see this as my big chance. I'd build my own egg business properly, maybe two or three sheds, all automated, selling direct and to the local shops. By 2036 I'd want to be the owner, not the manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the consulting and the vending hut for two or three years and save hard. Then around year three or four I'd buy land for my own unit and set it up with the best kit available. Sam and I would probably get the house with a garden too, because ten years is long enough to plan both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and actually excited. The worry's there, but it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bird flu, always. One outbreak and you lose the flock and months of income. The robots don't fix that, they just make the sheds cheaper to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young person starting out in poultry now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the birds properly first, then the tech, and save from day one. Owning something is the only safe thing in all of these pictures. That's what I've worked out talking to you, actually.

S4.say: She'd say that with ten years, any farm caught out has only itself to blame, keep running sessions for other producers and ask for a clear plan for rural jobs without expecting miracles.
S4.think: She sees ten years as her big chance to build her own automated egg business with two or three sheds and become the owner rather than the manager by 2036.
S4.do: Builds up consulting and the vending hut while saving hard for two or three years, then buys land for her own fully automated unit around year three or four, and buys a house with a garden with her partner.
S4.feel: Calm and excited, with only a small worry.
S4.quote: Owning something is the only safe thing in all of these pictures. That's what I've worked out talking to you, actually.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Jade's plans grow into full ownership and family plans move forward rather than back. Bird flu, not AI, remains her deepest business fear. She reached the 'ownership is safety' idea during the interview itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my edge disappears overnight. What would help is clear rules early, especially on animal welfare and who can own robot farms, and fair access to loans for small producers so it's not just the big packers buying everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to food prices. If eggs get really cheap because robots make them, great for shoppers, but people like me need to know whether it's still worth owning a shed.

headlineQuote: My whole edge is being early, and in two years everyone's early at once. I'd go from the clever one to the expensive one.
portrait: Jade Patel is a 27-year-old manager of a free-range egg unit who set up most of its cameras and AI tools herself and uses them every day. She's pragmatic and confident, with savings and plenty of nearby job options that she happily uses as bargaining power. In the slower pictures she plans to automate, consult and buy into the business. In the two-year picture she realises her edge disappears when everyone is early at once, and switches straight to owning sheds. Across all five, she works her way to one idea: owning something is the only safe position.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her advantage of being early would vanish overnight.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules set early, especially on welfare and ownership of robot farms, and fair access to loans for small producers.
